title: Venous thromboembolism: choosing the anticoagulant and how long

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the CHEST 2021 antithrombotic therapy for VTE guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: A deep vein thrombosis after hip surgery. How long is anticoagulation?
questions.why: A major transient provoking factor means the risk falls away once it has passed. The same three months applies to minor transient factors such as oestrogen or a long flight.

questions.q: A first unprovoked pulmonary embolism in a patient with low bleeding risk. How long is anticoagulation?
questions.a: Extended, with no scheduled stop date, reassessed each year
questions.why: Recurrence after stopping runs about 10% in the first year and 30% at five years. Bleeding risk and patient preference are reviewed annually rather than the drug being stopped by default.

questions.q: For most patients with venous thromboembolism and no cancer, which anticoagulant is preferred?
d: Low molecular weight heparin long term
questions.why: Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started alone with a loading phase; dabigatran and edoxaban need five to ten days of parenteral anticoagulation first.

questions.q: Venous thromboembolism in a patient with active cancer. Which is preferred?
questions.a: A direct oral anticoagulant or low molecular weight heparin, while the cancer is active
d: Three months of any agent then stop
questions.why: Low molecular weight heparin is favoured over rivaroxaban and edoxaban in gastrointestinal and genitourinary cancers because of bleeding at the tumour site; apixaban is the usual oral choice there.

questions.q: After 6 months of full-dose treatment, a patient continues extended anticoagulation. What dose is reasonable?
questions.a: Reduced dose: apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily
questions.why: Reduced dosing kept recurrence low with less bleeding in trials. Full dose stays for patients at high recurrence risk, such as those with antiphospholipid syndrome.

questions.q: Venous thromboembolism in a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome. Which anticoagulant?
questions.why: Direct oral anticoagulants had more arterial events than warfarin in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, so warfarin remains the standard there.

questions.q: An isolated distal calf vein thrombosis in a patient with mild symptoms and no risk factors for extension. Which option is reasonable?
questions.a: Serial ultrasound over two weeks rather than immediate anticoagulation
d: Three months of anticoagulation is mandatory
questions.why: If the clot extends, or if symptoms are severe or risk factors present, anticoagulation is given as for a proximal thrombosis.

questions.q: A second unprovoked venous thromboembolism. How long is anticoagulation?
questions.why: Two unprovoked events mark a patient whose recurrence risk stays high. Only a high bleeding risk argues for stopping.

questions.q: A haemodynamically stable patient with a low-risk pulmonary embolism, a simplified PESI of zero, and good support at home. Where is treatment given?
questions.a: At home, or after a short observation period
d: In hospital for at least five days
In hospital until the D-dimer normalises
questions.why: Outpatient treatment is safe for low-risk PE with an oral anticoagulant that needs no lead-in. Right ventricular strain or a raised troponin changes that.

questions.q: When is an inferior vena cava filter indicated?
questions.a: Acute venous thromboembolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated
d: As an addition to anticoagulation in large clots
questions.why: Filters do not replace anticoagulation and are removed once anticoagulation becomes possible. Adding a filter to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrence in trials.

questions.q: Superficial vein thrombosis 8 cm long, near the saphenofemoral junction. How long is prophylactic-dose fondaparinux given?
questions.why: Superficial thrombosis of 5 cm or more carries a real risk of extending into the deep system; a clot within 3 cm of the junction is treated as a deep vein thrombosis.

questions.q: Which test can wait until well after acute treatment of a deep vein thrombosis has started?
d: A pregnancy test in a woman of childbearing age
questions.why: Thrombophilia results rarely change acute management and are distorted by the clot and the drug. They are considered later, and only if the result would change the duration decision.
